deep.reconstruction:
The page is one continuous numerical table. The argument x runs from 7.750 to 8.050 in steps of 0.002, in three blocks: 7.750-7.850, 7.850-7.950 and 7.950-8.050. A fourth block (8.050-8.150, reaching about 168 deg 3') is cut off at the right edge. It continues the previous page, which runs from 7.450 upward.

Each block has four columns:
(i) the argument x;
(ii) an angle v(x) in deg ' " given to 10^-5 arcsec;
(iii) the first difference D1(x) = v(x+0.002) - v(x) in arcseconds;
(iv) the second difference -D2 = D1(x-0.002) - D1(x), in units of 10^-5 ".
In columns (iii) and (iv), leading digits common to the entry above are omitted (e.g. '20' = 12120, '21166' = 87.21166).

Identification of the function (my reconstruction, by numerical fitting). Put tau = tan(v/2). At three points:
- x = 7.45: v = 160d11'19.378", tau = 5.7264, tau + tau^3/3 = 68.32, log10 = 1.83455.
- x = 7.75: v = 164d22'26.398", tau = 7.2876, tau + tau^3/3 = 136.30, log10 = 2.13450.
- x = 8.00: v = 167d09'06.480", tau = 8.8815, tau + tau^3/3 = 242.41, log10 = 2.38454.

In every case log10(tau + tau^3/3) = x - 5.61545 to within about 5e-5, my hand precision. The constant is log10(2 * 206264.8) = 5.6154551, where 206264.8 is the number of arcseconds in a radian (rho"). Solving directly at x = 8 gives v = 167d09'06.4", matching the table's 167d09'06.48".

Hence the table is
  tan(v/2) + (1/3) tan^3(v/2) = 10^x / (2 rho"),
equivalently 10^x (in arcseconds) = 2(tau + tau^3/3) radians.

This is Barker's equation for parabolic motion, k t / (sqrt(2) q^(3/2)) = tan(v/2) + (1/3) tan^3(v/2). So x = log10( sqrt(2) k t / q^(3/2) ) with Gauss's constant k expressed in arcseconds (k = 3548.19"). The table gives the true anomaly v in a parabolic orbit as a function of the logarithm of the time from perihelion. This is a high-precision 'logarithmic Barker table' for the far branch (v from about 160 deg to 168 deg), where the asymptotic behaviour 180 deg - v ~ const * 10^(-x/3) makes a log argument natural.

The differences serve two purposes: building the table by summing differences, and controlling it, since the second differences decrease smoothly from 0.14542 to 0.11124.

results.what: High-precision table of the parabolic true anomaly v (about 164-168 deg) versus x = log10 of 2(tan(v/2) + tan^3(v/2)/3) expressed in arcseconds, i.e. x = log(sqrt(2) k t q^(-3/2)) with k in arcseconds; step 0.002, with first and second differences.
results.modern_name: Table for Barker's equation (parabolic Kepler problem), logarithmic-argument form
results.usually_credited_to: Barker (1757) for the table of the parabolic equation; Halley/Euler for the equation itself

results.what: Construction and verification of the table by summing differences, with smooth second differences used as a check

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss is well known to have computed and used parabolic-motion (Barker-type) tables, e.g. in connection with Theoria Motus. The only notable features are the logarithmic argument, which suits large anomalies, and the very high precision (1e-5 arcsec). Both are routine computational craft, not a new result.
